result:
The proposed answer, (1 − λ)/log(1/λ), holds up under my own check of the argument, though I did not derive it independently of the solution's setup and I could not confirm it against a published result.

**Structure.** The tree is a spine with a finite dead-end finger of length i attached at (i,0). A cut time must be the unique crossing of a spine edge, because every finger edge is crossed an even number of times.

**Cut density.** From a spine vertex, the walk steps up the spine with weight 1, down with weight λ, and into the finger with weight 1. Finger excursions return almost surely, so the effective spine walk has up:down odds 1:λ. After first reaching level i+1, the probability of never returning to level i is 1−λ. By regeneration, the fraction of spine edges crossed exactly once is therefore 1−λ.

**Time scale.** Inside a finger the walk is biased toward the tip with ratio 1/λ. Escaping back to the base from the tip region takes time of order λ^{-i}. Each spine level has a constant probability of a deep excursion, so T_n, the time to first reach level n, satisfies (1/n) log T_n → log(1/λ) almost surely.

- The upper bound comes from Borel–Cantelli on the time spent in each finger.
- The lower bound comes from the many levels just below n, each with an independent constant chance of a deep excursion.

The number of levels reached by time N is then n(N) ~ log N / log(1/λ).

**Combination.** The cut count satisfies M(N) ≈ (1−λ) n(N), and cut status at levels far below n(N) is asymptotically independent of the large excursion times near n(N). This gives

lim M(N)/log N = (1−λ)/log(1/λ).

VERDICT: ACCEPT
